```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
library(here)
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
here::i_am("errata.qmd")

out <- function(f) read_csv(here("maintained", "output", f), show_col_types = FALSE)

t3 <- out("table_3_study1_gun_support.csv")
t4 <- out("table_4_study2_conditions.csv")
t6 <- out("table_6_study2_favor.csv")
t7 <- out("table_7_study3_conditions.csv")
t8 <- out("table_8_study3_support.csv")

# Every number in a corrected sentence below is computed here, from the deposited
# archive, at the time this document is rendered. That includes the numbers that were
# not wrong: a token carried over from the published sentence is inherited on trust,
# and rendering the whole sentence from the pipeline is what verifies it.
cell <- function(d, grp, trm, column = "estimate") {
  hits <- d[[column]][d$group == grp & d$term == trm]
  stopifnot(length(hits) == 1)
  hits
}

group_n <- function(d, grp) {
  hits <- unique(d$N[str_detect(d$group, grp)])
  stopifnot(length(hits) == 1)
  hits
}

# The article states its Study 3 scale-point effects to three decimals and its
# p-values to two, so the corrected sentences keep that precision. Minus signs are
# set as the en dash the published page uses.
pt3 <- function(x) str_replace(sprintf("%.3f", x), "^-", "–")
pt2 <- function(x) str_replace(sprintf("%.2f", x), "^-", "–")
comma <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)

swing <- function(d, grp) {
  2 * (cell(d, grp, "positive_information") - cell(d, grp, "negative_information"))
}

opp_pos <- cell(t8, "Opponents (Covariates)", "positive_information")
opp_neg <- cell(t8, "Opponents (Covariates)", "negative_information")
opp_p <- cell(t8, "Opponents (Covariates)", "negative_information", "p.value")
pro_pos <- cell(t8, "Proponents (Covariates)", "positive_information")
pro_neg <- cell(t8, "Proponents (Covariates)", "negative_information")
```

This note lists eight corrections to "Does Counter-Attitudinal Information Cause Backlash? Results from Three Large Survey Experiments," published in the *British Journal of Political Science* 50(4), doi [10.1017/S0007123418000327](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0007123418000327). **None of them changes a conclusion of the paper.** The first is a table printed in place of another; three are participant counts that disagree with the article's own tables; three are Study 3 estimates restated in the text at a precision the tables do not show; and one is a cross-reference. The article's finding, that treatment effects across all three experiments run in the direction of the information rather than against it, is unaffected, and Figure 1 already plots the corrected Table 6 estimates rather than the ones that table prints.

A separate corrigendum, published at *British Journal of Political Science* 50(4), 1517, doi [10.1017/S0007123419000024](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0007123419000024), corrects the standard deviations of Table 1. That correction is not repeated here.

Every number in a corrected sentence below is computed from the deposited replication archive ([10.7910/DVN/J7WNTM](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/J7WNTM)) at the time this document is rendered, including the numbers that were not wrong. The code and output supporting each correction are at [github.com/active-maintenance-aec/guess_coppock_2020](https://github.com/active-maintenance-aec/guess_coppock_2020). Bold marks what has changed.

One published figure is deliberately absent from this list. The article reports that "93 per cent of subjects have a positive treatment effect estimate when exposed to positive information." The deposited BART script sets no seed, so that figure is a single unseeded draw and the right comparison is against the spread of draws rather than against a point. Refitting at ten seeds under a current sampler puts the proportion between 97.7 and 99.6 per cent, above the published figure in every run, which is a discrepancy worth recording but not a number that can be corrected to a value the analysis would reproduce. It is documented in the repository's report instead.

## 1. Table 6 reprints Table 5

Table 6, "Effects of information on favoring minimum wage raise," prints the contents of Table 5 rather than its own. Every cell is identical to Table 5's, and the column header inside Table 6 reads "Dependent variable: T2 Amount" where the table is captioned for the Favor outcome. The text is correct and the table is not: the deposited `GC_Study_2_analysis.R` fits its Table 6 models on `favor_T2_recode`, and Figure 1's "Study 2: T2 Favor" panel plots the estimates below rather than the ones Table 6 prints. The corrected table follows.

```{r table6}
star <- function(p) {
  case_when(p < 0.01 ~ "***", p < 0.05 ~ "**", p < 0.1 ~ "*", .default = "")
}

fmt <- function(est, p) paste0(str_replace(sprintf("%.2f", est), "^-", "–"), star(p))
fmt_se <- function(se) paste0("(", sprintf("%.2f", se), ")")

label_of <- c("positive_information" = "Pos. Info (0 to 1)",
              "negative_information" = "Neg. Info (0 to 1)",
              `I(condition_type == "Placebo")TRUE` = "Condition: Placebo",
              "(Intercept)" = "Constant")

groups <- c("Opponents (No Covariates)", "Opponents (Covariates)",
            "Moderates (No Covariates)", "Moderates (Covariates)",
            "Proponents (No Covariates)", "Proponents (Covariates)")

body <- map(names(label_of), function(trm) {
  est <- map_chr(groups, ~ fmt(cell(t6, .x, trm), cell(t6, .x, trm, "p.value")))
  se <- map_chr(groups, ~ fmt_se(cell(t6, .x, trm, "std.error")))
  bind_rows(
    tibble(term = label_of[[trm]], value = est, group = groups),
    tibble(term = "", value = se, group = groups)
  ) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = value)
}) |>
  list_rbind()

covar <- tibble(term = "Covariates") |>
  bind_cols(as_tibble(setNames(as.list(rep(c("No", "Yes"), 3)), groups)))
ns <- tibble(term = "N") |>
  bind_cols(as_tibble(setNames(as.list(map_chr(groups, ~ as.character(unique(t6$N[t6$group == .x])))), groups)))
r2 <- tibble(term = "$R^2$") |>
  bind_cols(as_tibble(setNames(as.list(map_chr(groups, function(g) {
    sprintf("%.2f", unique(t6$r2[t6$group == g]))
  })), groups)))

tab <- bind_rows(body, covar, ns, r2)

kable(tab, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", escape = FALSE,
      align = c("l", rep("r", 6)), col.names = c(" ", rep(c("", ""), 3)),
      caption = "Table 6, corrected. Effects of information on favoring minimum wage raise. Dependent variable: T2 Favor. Robust standard errors are in parentheses. The information content of the Placebo condition is coded 0. Covariates include T1 Amount, T1 Favor, age, gender, ideology, party ID, and education. *p < 0.1; **p < 0.05; ***p < 0.01") |>
  kableExtra::add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Among opponents" = 2, "Among moderates" = 2,
                                 "Among proponents" = 2), escape = FALSE) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

## 2. The Study 3 participant counts

> A total of **683** subjects participated in the main survey (287 proponents and **396** opponents).

Corrected:

> A total of **`r sum(t7$n)`** subjects participated in the main survey (287 proponents and **`r group_n(t8, "Opponents")`** opponents).

The article's own Table 7 gives the six condition sizes as 117, 116, 112, 118, 121 and 102, which sum to `r sum(t7$n)`, and Tables 8 and 9 report `r group_n(t8, "Opponents")` opponents. The deposited Study 3 data hold `r sum(t7$n)` rows, of which `r group_n(t8, "Proponents")` are proponents, `r group_n(t8, "Opponents")` are opponents, and four carry no pre-treatment classification and so appear in Table 7 but in neither regression table.

## 3. The Study 2 participant count

> Of the 1,500 recruited to the main survey, **1,170** participated.

Corrected:

> Of the 1,500 recruited to the main survey, **`r comma(sum(t4$n))`** participated.

The article's own Table 4 gives the seven condition sizes as 93, 162, 165, 195, 169, 192 and 193, which sum to `r comma(sum(t4$n))`, and the deposited Study 2 data hold `r comma(sum(t4$n))` rows.

## 4. The Study 3 positive information estimate among opponents

> Focusing on the covariate-adjusted models, we estimate that a one-unit increase in positive information causes an average increase in support for capital punishment of 0.015 scale points among proponents and **0.068** scale points among opponents, neither of which is statistically significant.

Corrected:

> Focusing on the covariate-adjusted models, we estimate that a one-unit increase in positive information causes an average increase in support for capital punishment of `r pt3(pro_pos)` scale points among proponents and **`r pt3(opp_pos)`** scale points among opponents, neither of which is statistically significant.

The published sentence gives 0.068 for opponents. The specification the deposit fits, and which Table 8's fourth column reports, gives `r pt3(opp_pos)`. Both round to the 0.07 that Table 8 prints, so the disagreement is visible only at the precision the text itself uses. Dropping race from the covariate set gives 0.086, so the published figure comes from neither specification.

## 5. The Study 3 negative information estimate among opponents

> Negative information has a strong negative effect among proponents (–0.326, p < 0.01), and a weakly negative effect among opponents (**–0.042**, p = **0.43**).

Corrected:

> Negative information has a strong negative effect among proponents (`r pt3(pro_neg)`, p < 0.01), and a weakly negative effect among opponents (**`r pt3(opp_neg)`**, p = **`r pt2(opp_p)`**).

The published sentence gives –0.042 and p = 0.43. Table 8's own fourth column, and the deposited specification behind it, give `r pt3(opp_neg)` with p = `r pt2(opp_p)`. The estimate is not significant at any conventional level on either figure.

## 6. The Study 3 movement from Con Con to Pro Pro among opponents

> These estimates imply that moving from the Con Con condition to the Pro Pro condition would cause proponents to move 2·0.015 + 2·0.326 = 0.682 scale points and opponents to move 2·**0.068** + 2·**0.042** = **0.220** scale points.

Corrected:

> These estimates imply that moving from the Con Con condition to the Pro Pro condition would cause proponents to move 2·`r pt3(pro_pos)` + 2·`r pt3(abs(pro_neg))` = `r pt3(swing(t8, "Proponents (Covariates)"))` scale points and opponents to move 2·**`r pt3(opp_pos)`** + 2·**`r pt3(abs(opp_neg))`** = **`r pt3(swing(t8, "Opponents (Covariates)"))`** scale points.

The published sentence gives 2·0.068 + 2·0.042 = 0.220. The arithmetic is right and the two inputs are the ones corrected in entries 4 and 5, so the total moves with them.

## 7. The cross-reference to the binary support results

> In **Table 2**, we turn to the binary gun control support dependent variable, which asks whether respondents support 'stricter gun control laws in the United States.'

Corrected:

> In **Table 3**, we turn to the binary gun control support dependent variable, which asks whether respondents support 'stricter gun control laws in the United States.'

Table 2 is the composite scale table, discussed in the preceding paragraph, which opens with the same words. The binary support models are Table 3.

## 8. The significance threshold in the Table 2 note

> \*p < 0.1; \*\*p < 0.05; \*\*\*p **>** 0.01

Corrected:

> \*p < 0.1; \*\*p < 0.05; \*\*\*p **<** 0.01

Three stars mark the most significant cells, not the least. Table 3's note, on the facing page, states the same threshold correctly. The starred cells are unaffected: the three-star coefficients in these tables have p-values of `r sprintf("%.4f", cell(t3, "Among Proponents (No Covariates)", "Z_informationcon_information", "p.value"))` and below.
